title: Harsh clashing sound
core: All three name noise that hurts — sound the speaker has already judged unpleasant, not merely loud. What separates them is *why* it hurts: too many sounds at odds with each other, one resonant metallic sound hammering on, or one thin high note drilling in. Only one is a neutral description of a sound source; the other two are verdicts, and one of those is routinely aimed at people rather than noises.

words.nuance: **Cacophonous** requires *plurality and disagreement* — horns plus drills plus shouting, sounds that refuse to blend. A single unbearable noise, however loud or high, cannot be cacophonous, which is why it's the only one of the three that transfers cleanly to clashing colours or a mess of contradictory opinions.

**Clangor** is a noun naming a specific *texture*: metallic, resonant, with a ring in its tail — bells, hammers, armour — and sustained rather than momentary. It's the only member that identifies what the sound is made of rather than delivering a verdict on taste, and its literary, industrial-martial register means it appears in prose describing a battlefield or foundry, never in a noise complaint.

**Shrill** is about *pitch*, not quantity or material: one thin, high, piercing note. It's also the only one that attacks a person — calling a critic or campaign shrill dismisses the tone to avoid the substance, and it reveals the speaker's irritation more than the target's logic.

exam_note: The trap is treating all three as synonyms for "very loud": GRE contexts hinge on discord (cacophonous), metal (clangor), or pitch-and-tone-policing (shrill) — and in reading comp, an author calling an opponent shrill is a signal about the author's bias, not the opponent's volume.
